lessons.question: Twelve cases go in. Nine pass first time, two need help, one is stuck. A slide says 100% success on completed cases. Fair?
options: Yes, the nine completed cases all passed
No, it hides the cases that needed help
Yes, if the stuck case is retried later
lessons.explanation: Reporting 9/9 quietly drops the three hardest cases. Honest reporting keeps all twelve in the denominator and explains what the human corrections changed.

lessons.after: For each case record input reference
lessons.prompt: Should each moment be logged as active staff minutes or as waiting time?

items.text: Reviewer checks the draft against sources
Draft sits in a queue with no reviewer assigned
Case waits overnight for the next shift

lessons.explanation: A fast run can still give poor service if it waits a day for review. Logging the two timings separately shows where end-to-end delay really comes from.

lessons.question: In the worked pilot, what percentage of the twelve cases needed human correction to complete? Round to one decimal place.
lessons.explanation: Two of twelve cases completed after correction: 2 / 12 × 100 ≈ 16.7%. This correction workload belongs in the report alongside first-pass and final success.

lessons.after: If all twelve cases came from the fictional pack
lessons.question: Your pilot moves from fictional cases to real users. What must you now record?
options: Nothing new, the process is the same
Their consent and authorised data use
lessons.explanation: Real users bring real data and real people. Consent and authorised data use must be recorded through the organisation's normal process.

lessons.question: You spot a bad output during the pilot. Before changing anything, what is most worth keeping?
options: A case that reproduces the failure
A screenshot of your best output
lessons.explanation: A reproduction case lets you confirm the fix actually works and becomes a regression test. Without it, you cannot tell whether the failure is gone or just hiding.

lessons.prompt: Which stage does each Harbour failure most likely belong to?

items.text: A sales row has a missing amount
A draft policy reaches the generator
The same external action happens twice
A transaction uses an unrecognised currency
Nobody can tell if a timed-out action ran

lessons.explanation: Naming the stage points you to the right fix. A duplicate action is an idempotency issue and a wrong source is a filter issue, so rewriting the prompt would help neither.

lessons.prompt: Arrange the improvement loop in the order this lesson describes.
lessons.explanation: Diagnosis comes before change, and a single targeted change makes it clear what caused any improvement. The rerun confirms the fix without breaking other cases.

lessons.after: The report includes the draft automatic-refund proposal.
lessons.prompt: Why should the new regression case contain a highly relevant draft, rather than any old draft?
lessons.answer: The draft slipped through because it looked relevant. A highly relevant draft is the hardest test of the status filter, so passing it shows status, not just relevance, now decides what reaches the generator.

lessons.prompt: Your pilot shows the system does not pay off. Could that recommendation still earn full credit? Decide, then reveal.
lessons.answer: Yes. A pilot that recommends stopping can earn full credit if it uses a working system and sound evidence. Positive ROI is not required; honest measurement and a defensible decision are.

lessons.after: Run the bounded pilot with instrumentation
lessons.question: Which mix of traces does the engineering route ask you to review?
options: A success, a corrected result and a failure
Every trace from the development set
lessons.explanation: Comparing a success, a corrected case and a failure shows how the system behaves across outcomes. Looking only at one kind hides the contrast that explains defects.

lessons.after: Observe users completing the actual review task.
lessons.prompt: Which route does each pilot-review task belong to?

items.text: Fix the top defect and keep its regression case
Ask users where they felt uncertain
Rehearse rollback or stopping new work
Check whether users ignored unresolved items
Update cost sensitivity using observed workload

lessons.explanation: Engineers fix and verify the system; business owners watch how people actually use it and what it costs. Both feed the updated decision record.

lessons.prompt: Name the three things to confirm before moving on to handover.
lessons.answer: Unresolved cases have owners, the pilot stayed within its authorised scope, and final evaluation claims are independent of the development examples used for tuning.
